articles.title: Biotic and abiotic drivers of ecosystem functioning differ between a temperate and a tropical region
articles.desc: Any single ecosystem will provide many ecosystem functions. Yet, we lack large‐scale, systematic studies of how abiotic factors can directly or indirectly – via effects on biodiversity – drive ecosystem functioning. In this study, we assessed the impact of climate, landscape and biotic community on ecosystem functioning in the temperate and tropical zone, with potential trade‐offs among ecosystem functions in both zones. To this aim, we measured a diverse set of insect‐related functions – including herbivory, seed dispersal, predation, decomposition and pollination – at 50 sites across Madagascar and 171 sites across Sweden, while characterizing the insect community at each site. For the temperate zone, we found that abiotic factors were most important in driving ecosystem functioning, while in the tropical zone, effects of biotic drivers were most pronounced. In the temperate zone, most functions were uncorrelated, but in the tropical zone, most ecosystem functions increased in concert. Our study suggests that the functioning of temperate and tropical ecosystems differs fundamentally in terms of patterns and drivers. To identify global patterns and drivers of ecosystem functioning, and to predict future ecosystem functioning, we next need further replication across biomes.

Objectives We modeled and mapped suitable wildcat habitats at the continental scale, to identify opportunities and constraints for its conservation. Methods We compiled a large telemetry dataset comprising 200 wildcats across Europe and developed multi-scale habitat suitability models using Maxent. Habitat selection was analyzed at two hierarchical levels: home-range placement within the wider landscape and selection within the established home ranges. Results At both levels, wildcats selected broadleaved forests, mixed forests, and grasslands, while avoiding landscapes dominated by large continuous forests. For home-range placement, they preferred lower terrain ruggedness and less intensive agriculture. Within the home ranges, wildcats selected forest edges and small woody features. articles.desc: Context Jack pine budworm (JPBW), Choristoneura pinus pinus, is a major defoliator in Canada, yet remains absent from theoretical discourse on outbreak synchrony, despite sharing key life history traits with the archetypal “cross-scale” pest, spruce budworm (C. fumiferana). JPBW has primarily been studied in host-rich landscapes, raising questions about its behavior in host-sparse regions. Methods We applied a systematic framework for analyzing spatiotemporal tree-ring data, adapted from recent reconstructions of spruce budworm and forest tent caterpillar. Protecting birds in protected areas: a multi-scale analysis of forest structure and species occurrence
articles.desc: Protected areas are cornerstones of avian conservation, yet forest-associated bird communities continue to decline even within protected lands. The capacity of a protected area to sustain bird populations depends on both internal habitat quality and the surrounding landscape context, yet the relative importance of these scales remains poorly understood. We evaluate how forest structure at three nested spatial scales (local, park, and county) influences the occurrence of forest-associated birds within protected areas. articles.title: Over 20 years of GIAHS. A perspective on the impact and future development of the FAO Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems Programme
articles.desc: The Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS) Programme is a flagship initiative of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), aimed at identifying and preserving Agricultural Heritage Systems for future generations. GIAHS represent a rural development model based on dynamic conservation principles, provisioning of ecosystem services, and sustainability. This perspective paper aims to assess the evolution, impacts, and future development of the GIAHS Programme after more than 20 years since its establishment. To ensure the long-term effectiveness of the GIAHS Programme, we suggest to: i) identify an official management organization for each site; ii) implement a mandatory monitoring system based on standardized social, economic and environmental indicators; iii) promote the transition to participatory, bottom-up governance; iv) promote educational and training activities and upskilling of stakeholders; v) integrate tourism and dynamic conservation management through multi-stakeholder Action Plans; vi) strengthen the synergies among GIAHS sites for research activities, peer-to-peer learning, and best practices exchange. articles.desc: Context Biological invasions are deemed to be the second most important global driver of biodiversity loss showing strong interactions with the aftermaths of land use change and landscape fragmentation. The role of landscape composition and configuration in biological invasions is widely considered while its interplay with landscape connectivity is less understood. articles.desc: Context Termites, like other pattern-generating organisms, often create vegetation heterogeneity. articles.desc: Context Urban and nearby non-urban landscapes differ in vegetation and surface climate. How these differences vary with hydroclimate over multiple decades remains poorly resolved. articles.desc: Context. Mangrove protection and restoration are increasingly prioritized as nature-based solutions for climate mitigation, coastal resilience, and livelihood support. articles.desc: Context Home-ranging is common among animal species, as site fidelity facilitates cognitive map development and promotes efficient habitat use. The adaptive value of site fidelity, however, should decline as environmental conditions change, yet empirical evidence remains limited. Objectives We investigated how fire and forest harvesting affect home-range stability in boreal caribou, a species typically exhibiting strong site fidelity. articles.desc: Context Ecological corridors that are high in biodiversity potential and stable under climate change are central to long-term conservation planning. Objectives We aimed to develop an ecological connectivity framework that jointly incorporates land-use resistance and climate stability to map linkages among protected areas, and to quantify and communicate methodological uncertainty arising from key parameterization choices. articles.desc: Context Riparian vegetation is a major driver of freshwater biodiversity; however, the structural degradation of riparian vegetation due to anthropogenic pressures poses a major threat to riverine ecosystems worldwide. articles.desc: Spatial clusters of animal nests can be driven by mating behaviors, social benefits, and landscape heterogeneity. articles.desc: Community perceptions of ecosystem services are shaped by individuals’ local contexts and their direct interactions with the environment. articles.desc: Whereas acute stress responses support immediate escape from transient threats, persistent or repeated predation risk (hereafter referred to as chronic predation risk) requires organisms to continually reallocate limited energetic resources among competing physiological demands. Classical stress physiology emphasizes acute "fight-or-flight" responses that transiently mobilize glucose and lipids to skeletal muscle, whereas life‑history and allostatic‑load frameworks highlight long‑term trade-offs between survival, growth, and reproduction. Yet these perspectives rarely specify how energy is redistributed among tissues under persistent threat. Here, we synthesize life-history theory, stress physiology, evolutionary medicine, and recent experimental work in a predator-exposed Drosophila melanogaster model to propose Threat-Induced Neural Prioritization (TINP), a conceptual framework describing how persistent predation risk induces tissue-specific metabolic reorganization that preferentially allocates energetic resources to neural and glial tissues. This reprogramming supports energetically costly processes such as memory consolidation and decision‑making that enhance survival, but reduces investment in peripheral homeostasis and can shade into pathology under environmental mismatch. The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
articles.desc: Carbon removal markets lack a standardized, quantitative measure of permanence risk. Inspired by value at risk in financial markets, we propose carbon at risk (CaR): a probabilistic measure of the shortfall between contracted removals and realized storage at a given confidence level and time horizon. We calibrate CaR in two proof-of-concept applications: forest carbon, where Monte Carlo simulations driven by satellite fire data yield a single-project 95% CaR of more than 70% over 200 years for California, and geological storage, where simulations using the Storage Security Calculator show that the 95% CaR ranges from 0.15% (well-regulated offshore) to 17% (poorly regulated onshore). Combining technologies in a portfolio can help manage tail risk cost-effectively. The minimum cost of meeting a permanence target depends on the magnitude and correlation structure of key risk factors. CaR provides a technology-agnostic basis for risk-calibrated buffer sizing, insurance pricing and reserve-fund design, over both policy- and climate-relevant horizons.
